docs.title: GitHub SDLC Automation with IBM Bob
i. GitHub is the connective tissue of modern software delivery
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) introduces the GitHub SDLC Automation with IBM Bob curriculum for hands-on enablement. [6 min]

For the last decade, GitHub has become the connective tissue of modern software engineering. Issues capture requirements, pull requests carry code review, Actions drive continuous integration & continuous delivery (CI/CD), and branches organize the work in-between.

Typical GitHub-centered workloads include:

  • Web and mobile front-end applications
  • Backend services and REST APIs
  • Data pipelines and analytics tooling
  • Infrastructure-as-code and platform engineering
  • Internal developer tools and dashboards
  • Open-source libraries and SDKs

Despite the maturity of the tooling, most teams still feel the same friction:

  • Requirements buried in long issue threads
  • Time-consuming code reviews that block delivery
  • Inconsistent PR descriptions and commit hygiene
  • Context switching between the IDE, the browser, and the terminal
  • Uneven test coverage and validation habits
  • A widening gap between what a codebase does and what its docs say

Whether a team is shipping a mobile app, a data platform, or an internal microservice, the workflow tends to look the same: an issue is opened, a branch is created, code is written, tests run, a pull request is reviewed, and — eventually — something is merged and deployed.

It is precisely this friction that IBM Bob was designed to relieve.

docs.title: ii. What is IBM Bob?
docs.text:
RECOMMENDED PREREQUISITE: CLIMBING THE AI MATURITY CURVE

This course assumes you have completed the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve with IBM Bob Level 3 curriculum, and it assumes those concepts are familiar ground: the Agentic Sidebar and its modes, the plan-first delegation discipline, Bob Rules, and the context economics that govern every session. The material ahead builds directly upon that foundation— the discipline you practiced there is precisely what this lab applies to the GitHub delivery loop.

IBM Bob is an AI-powered software engineering partner that supports the entire software development lifecycle (SDLC). Where a traditional code-completion tool is anchored to the current line, Bob is designed to participate in the actual delivery loop — reading a repository, understanding a GitHub issue, implementing a targeted change, running tests, reviewing its own diff, and preparing a merge-ready pull request.

For GitHub-centered teams, Bob can:

  • Analyze a repository's structure and propose an implementation plan
  • Scaffold a new application from a description of the target outcome
  • Integrate external APIs and data sources
  • Generate UI components, service layers, and tests
  • Run project validation and interpret the failures
  • Summarize git diff output into clean commit and PR descriptions
  • Fetch and interpret GitHub issues as scoped work items
  • Perform code review with issue-coverage checks
  • Prepare branches for merge or automated closure

Bob operates inside a VS Code-based IDE with direct access to your Git working tree and GitHub context. Every conversation is grounded in the current state of the repository — the branch, the diff, the open issues, the CI results.

docs.title: iii. The environment
docs.text:
The application used throughout this workshop is a React-based finance dashboard that tracks IBM and a small set of major competitors — Microsoft, Oracle, SAP, and Salesforce — using publicly available market data from Yahoo Finance.

The app is intentionally small enough to build in one sitting and realistic enough to demonstrate the full delivery loop. It contains the pieces most modern web applications rely on:

Component Responsibility Dashboard page Top-level layout for the three time-window views Chart cards Reusable components for current day, 7-day, and quarterly trends Finance data service Yahoo Finance integration with response normalization Company registry Configurable set of tracked ticker symbols Validation suite Unit tests for data transforms and one rendering path GitHub workflow CI pipeline for lint, test, and build on every push

Together, these components exercise the patterns that dominate real-world engineering:

  • Component-oriented React architecture
  • Service-layer separation between data and UI
  • External API integration with resilience to missing or partial data
  • Chart-based data visualization
  • Unit and rendering tests
  • GitHub-driven CI/CD

Although the app is small, it drives the same delivery workflow that larger teams use every day.

docs.title: iv. Objectives and outline
docs.text:
Modern engineering teams rarely struggle to write code. The struggle concentrates in the work around the code— understanding requirements, reviewing diffs, writing PR descriptions, keeping tests current, coordinating across issues —which consumes a disproportionate share of every sprint.

The hardest questions are usually:

  • What does this issue actually ask for?
  • Which files need to change?
  • What could this break?
  • Is the test coverage still meaningful?
  • Does the PR description reflect what was actually done?
  • Is this branch really ready to merge?

IBM Bob accelerates these activities by providing:

  • Repository-grounded analysis of the actual codebase
  • Direct access to Git and GitHub context
  • Guided workflows for scaffolding, review, and PR preparation
  • Auto-generated commit messages and PR descriptions from real diffs
  • Issue-coverage review to confirm a change matches its request
  • Guardrails that keep the developer in control at every step

All while keeping the engineer firmly in charge of what ships.

This workshop follows a realistic GitHub-driven delivery workflow. Rather than generating isolated snippets, you will use IBM Bob to perform the same activities engineering teams do every day — planning, building, testing, reviewing, and evolving an application through GitHub.

Part Focus What You'll Learn Part 1: Build Scaffold and deliver the initial application Use Bob to interpret the project goal, scaffold a React app, integrate Yahoo Finance data, build the dashboard views, add tests, and prepare a review-ready commit Part 2: Evolve Deliver enhancements through GitHub Push the app to GitHub, open an issue for a new feature, let Bob analyze the request, implement the change, validate it, and prepare a merge-ready pull request

Take note of the shape of this journey and how it relates to the topics covered within the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve with IBM Bob Level 3 curriculum.

  • Part 1 | Build is the plan-first delegation rhythm of Module 2 | Delegate applied at project scale — an implementation plan is agreed, then approved sub-task by sub-task, with Bob working autonomously between the gates.
  • Part 2 | Evolve operates at the far right of the curve, Module 4 | Scale & Extend — Bob's reach extends outward into GitHub itself (issues, CI, pull requests), while your control concentrates at the moments that matter most: the requirements gate, the push, and the merge. The instrument is unchanged from the previous course; what changes here is that the delivery loop itself becomes the workbench.

Each part builds on the previous one, demonstrating how AI can assist across the complete SDLC — from an empty repository to an application that ships changes through pull requests. By the end of the hands-on lab, you will have a working React finance dashboard backed by tests, a CI pipeline, and a GitHub-driven evolution loop.

docs.title: v. Next steps
docs.text:
In Part 1 | Build, you will build the initial finance dashboard from an empty repository. You'll use Bob to interpret the goal, scaffold the app, integrate Yahoo Finance data, build the dashboards, add tests, and prepare a clean set of Git changes.

In Part 2 | Evolve, you will push the app to GitHub and let Bob take over the evolution loop — fetching an issue, implementing a user-selected company chart, validating the result, and preparing a merge-ready pull request.

By the end, you will have seen IBM Bob participate in every stage of a modern software delivery workflow — an engineering partner operating inside the GitHub-centered delivery loop that most teams already use.

docs.title: 1.1 Planning and scaffolding the application
docs.text: PART 1 | BUILD

docs.title: i. Why this matters
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Planning and Scaffolding the Application module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

Before generating a single line of code, IBM Bob should understand what it is being asked to build. Scaffolding an application without that context tends to produce boilerplate that has to be thrown away — plausible React code that does not match the repository, the workshop goals, or the delivery workflow.

Modern GitHub-driven engineering follows the opposite pattern. A clear plan is drafted first. Component boundaries, service layers, state management, and validation strategy are agreed up front. Only then does implementation begin, and every file that lands in the repository maps to a decision that was made deliberately.

The application will track IBM and four major competitors — Microsoft, Oracle, SAP, and Salesforce — using Yahoo Finance data across three time windows: current day, last 7 days, and last quarter.

In this module, you will use IBM Bob to inspect the workshop starter repository, produce a structured implementation plan for a React finance dashboard, and then scaffold the application in a shape that supports later GitHub-driven feature evolution.

Pay attention to how Bob frames the greenfield task as an engineering exercise— folder layout, data-service boundaries, error handling, test strategy —rather than a code-generation shortcut.

docs.title: ii. Planning and scaffolding the application
docs.text:
ATTENTION: NON-DETERMINISTIC WORK AHEAD

Bob's responses are non-deterministic, so the plan and file layout produced in your IDE may differ from those shown here. It's also possible that some architectural choices — folder names, chart library, state management approach — will vary from run to run.

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against.

All this is to say: Your results ahead may vary. The key takeaway from these workflows is that you understand how to effectively utilize each of Bob's Modes and where their strengths are best applied. Whether or not you arrive at the exact same codebase at the end is of less importance. Bob will ensure either way that your application works and delivers more-or-less what you asked for. The exact implementation and steps that Bob takes to arrive at that result, however, may differ from the steps documented here.

The starter repository contains only the workshop scaffolding: documentation, a pull request template, and a CI workflow. Everything else, including the React project itself, will be generated by Bob.

You will move through this module in two phases. First to ask Bob to analyze the repository and propose an implementation plan. Then to approve the plan and let Bob scaffold the application sub-task by sub-task. By the end of the module, the app will run locally in mock mode and render its first dashboard view.

  1. Open the workshop repository inside the Bob IDE.

    • Click the Explorer tab along the left edge of the IDE.
    • If no folder is currently open, click the Open Folder button to expose the file picker.
    • Navigate to the GitHub SDLC Automation folder from the Setup module, select it, and click Open.
    • Bob will load the workspace, index the repository, and prepare the Agentic Sidebar.

  1. With Agent mode active, copy and paste the following task into the Agentic Sidebar session window. This is the analysis and planning prompt for the entire finance dashboard.

    Analyze this repository as the starting point for a new React-based finance analytics lab. Propose an implementation plan for a market dashboard application that tracks IBM and up to four competitors using Yahoo Finance data. The application should present three time-window views: current day, last 7 days, and last quarter. Recommend a practical architecture including source folders, React component boundaries, data service abstractions, charting approach, state management strategy, error handling, test strategy, and local validation steps. Also explain how the implementation should support later GitHub-driven feature evolution through issues and pull requests.

    With the prompt entered, hit Enter or press the Send button to the right of the chat interface.

  1. Bob will explore the repository, then produce a rich HTML implementation plan. The Agentic Sidebar will summarize the key architecture decisions: source layout, component boundaries, data service, charting, state management, error handling, test strategy, and GitHub evolution model.

    • Click Open on the Market Dashboard — Implementation Plan report to review the full plan in the IDE.
    • The generated plan opens directly inside the Bob IDE as a self-contained HTML report. It covers the application overview, source folder layout, component boundaries, data-service architecture, and the GitHub evolution model that Part 2 | Evolve will build on.
    • Scroll through the report and confirm that the plan matches the workshop goal before moving on. This is the last checkpoint before Bob starts writing code.

  1. With the plan reviewed, ask Bob to scaffold the application. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar:

    Create a simple React application structure for this repository. Include a dashboard page, reusable chart card components, a finance data service layer, and a clean folder layout suitable for future enhancements.

    Press Enter to submit the task for execution within the Agentic Sidebar.

  1. After submitting your scaffolding request, Bob will first re-read the implementation plan and generate a detailed execution roadmap presented as a Todo List.

    • Review the proposed plan carefully to ensure it aligns with the folder layout, component boundaries, and validation strategy from the plan
    • Once the plan has been reviewed, click Approve todo tools for task

    Bob will begin executing the scaffolding workflow. During implementation, Bob may request approval before performing certain actions such as creating files, modifying source code, running build commands, executing tests, or installing dependencies. Review these requests and approve them as needed.

    Bob will generate an Update Todo List with the following (or similar) sub-tasks:

    TASK OBJECTIVES Sub-Task 1 Scaffold React app with Vite + TypeScript Sub-Task 2 Create constants, types, and mock data Sub-Task 3 Implement data service layer Sub-Task 4 Implement custom hooks Sub-Task 5 Build layout components Sub-Task 6 Build feedback components Sub-Task 7 Build card components Sub-Task 8 Build chart components Sub-Task 9 Build view components Sub-Task 10 Wire up App shell, tests, and configuration Sub-Task 11 Run local validation (lint + test + build)

SEQUENCING THE SUB-TASKS

In the steps ahead, you will examine in detail what each Sub-Task is performing and understand the rationale for the change. With your approval, Bob will then go ahead and implement the work on your behalf.

Sub-Task 1: Scaffold React App with Vite + TypeScript

Before writing any application code, Bob initializes a new React 18 project using Vite as the build tool and TypeScript for type safety. This establishes the base package.json, tsconfig.json, index.html, and entry point files that every other sub-task will build on.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 1. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 1 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 1 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 1 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Project Initialization: Created a Vite + React 18 + TypeScript project inside finance-app/ with base package.json, tsconfig.json, index.html, and src/main.tsx entry point.
    • Base Configuration: Established the build toolchain, dev server configuration, and TypeScript strict mode settings for the project.

Sub-Task 2: Create Constants, Types, and Mock Data

Bob establishes the domain foundation for the application. This includes the COMPANIES registry (the single source of truth for tracked tickers), TypeScript types for Quote, HistoryPoint, and TimeWindow, and deterministic mock fixtures that let the app run offline during tests and development.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 2. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 2 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 2 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 2 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Company Registry: Created constants/companies.ts with the five tracked tickers (IBM, MSFT, ORCL, SAP, CRM) as the single source of truth.
    • Domain Types: Established types/finance.ts with Quote, HistoryPoint, and TimeWindow types used across the service, hook, and view layers.
    • Mock Fixtures: Created deterministic seeded mock data so the app can run and be tested without external network access.

Sub-Task 3: Implement Data Service Layer

Bob creates the data-access layer with a clean separation of concerns: financeService.ts exposes the public API, yahooAdapter.ts maps raw Yahoo Finance responses to domain types, and mockData.ts supplies deterministic fixtures. This isolation keeps the UI independent of the data source and makes swapping providers a one-file change.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 3. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 3 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 3 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 3 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Public Service Interface: Created services/financeService.ts as the sole entry point for quote and history fetching.
    • Yahoo Adapter: Implemented services/yahooAdapter.ts to map raw API responses into the domain model, with null-safe handling for missing optional fields.
    • Mock/Live Seam: Wired the service to switch between live and mock data based on the VITE_USE_MOCK environment variable.

Sub-Task 4: Implement Custom Hooks

Bob creates two custom React hooks that encapsulate all data-fetching state: useQuotes returns current-day quotes for all tracked tickers with loading and error states, and useHistory returns historical time-series data for a given TimeWindow. Views remain pure props-in / render-out, which makes them trivial to test.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 4. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 4 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 4 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 4 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • useQuotes Hook: Created hooks/useQuotes.ts to fetch current-day quotes for all tracked tickers with idle, loading, error, and success states.
    • useHistory Hook: Created hooks/useHistory.ts to fetch historical time series scoped by TimeWindow ('7d' or 'quarter').

Sub-Task 5: Build Layout Components

Bob builds the shell components that frame the application. Header provides the IBM-blue banner with the app title and a refresh action, and TabBar provides the Day / 7 Days / Quarter navigation.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 5. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 5 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 5 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 5 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Header Component: Created components/layout/Header.tsx with IBM-blue styling, application title, last-refresh timestamp, and refresh action.
    • TabBar Component: Created components/layout/TabBar.tsx with the three time-window tabs and active-state styling.

Sub-Task 6: Build Feedback Components

Bob builds the reusable feedback surfaces that every view will rely on: LoadingSpinner for pending states (with an ARIA role for accessibility) and ErrorBanner for failed fetches (with a retry action).

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 6. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 6 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 6 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 6 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • LoadingSpinner Component: Created components/feedback/LoadingSpinner.tsx with animated indicator and accessible ARIA role.
    • ErrorBanner Component: Created components/feedback/ErrorBanner.tsx with warning styling and a retry callback.

Sub-Task 7: Build Card Components

Bob builds the reusable card primitives — QuoteCard renders a single ticker's price and change, and QuoteCardGrid arranges the cards in a responsive grid that adapts across screen sizes.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 7. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 7 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 7 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 7 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • QuoteCard Component: Created components/cards/QuoteCard.tsx displaying ticker, price, change amount, change percentage, and volume with color-coded gain/loss styling.
    • QuoteCardGrid Component: Created components/cards/QuoteCardGrid.tsx as a responsive grid wrapper for the current-day view.

Sub-Task 8: Build Chart Components

Bob builds the visualization components using Recharts. LineChart renders the 7-day trend with all tickers rebased to an index of 100 for direct comparison. AreaChart renders the 13-week quarterly trend. ChartLegend provides a color-coded company legend shared across both charts.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 8. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 8 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 8 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 8 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • LineChart Component: Created components/charts/LineChart.tsx with a Recharts responsive container and normalization to a base-100 index.
    • AreaChart Component: Created components/charts/AreaChart.tsx for the quarterly view with a stacked area presentation.
    • ChartLegend Component: Created components/charts/ChartLegend.tsx with a color-coded strip identifying each tracked company.

Sub-Task 9: Build View Components

Bob assembles the three time-window views. Each view is a thin composition of the hooks and components already built: CurrentDayView renders QuoteCardGrid via useQuotes, WeekView renders LineChart via useHistory('7d'), and QuarterView renders AreaChart via useHistory('quarter').

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 9. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 9 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 9 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 9 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • CurrentDayView: Created views/CurrentDayView.tsx composing quote cards via useQuotes with loading and error surfaces.
    • WeekView: Created views/WeekView.tsx rendering the rebased line chart via useHistory('7d').
    • QuarterView: Created views/QuarterView.tsx rendering the quarterly area chart via useHistory('quarter').

Sub-Task 10: Wire Up App Shell, Tests, and Configuration

Bob wires everything together in App.tsx — the shell composes the Header, TabBar, active view, and an ErrorBoundary. Bob then adds unit tests for the data adapter, mock fixtures, and one card component, plus configuration files (ESLint, .gitignore, .env.example) that the CI workflow depends on.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 10. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 10 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 10 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 10 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • App Shell: Created src/App.tsx with active-view state management, ErrorBoundary wrapper, and global styles.
    • Test Suite: Added unit tests for the yahoo adapter, mock data determinism, and a QuoteCard rendering path using Testing Library and jest-dom.
    • Configuration Files: Added ESLint config, .gitignore, and .env.example documenting the VITE_USE_MOCK environment variable.

Sub-Task 11: Run Local Validation

Bob runs a complete validation cycle — ESLint, the Jest test suite, and the TypeScript build — to confirm the scaffold compiles cleanly, every test passes, and no linting issues remain. This is the last gate before the app is considered scaffold-complete.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, you will be prompted with the following: Ready to implement Sub-Task 11. Shall I go ahead?

    If you agree with the changes, type Yes and Enter to approve Sub-Task 11 execution.

  1. Continue approving any additional requests related to Sub-Task 11 until the Agentic Sidebar chat has reported back with a summary of Sub-Task 11 is done. Here's what has changed.

    • Validation Gate: Executed npm run lint, npm test, and npm run build to compile the application and validate all generated code.
    • Scaffold Verification: Confirmed zero lint errors, all tests passing, and a clean TypeScript build — demonstrating that the scaffold is ready to run and to be extended in the next module.

  1. At this stage, all eleven sub-tasks have been completed and validated. Bob will present a full file inventory of the generated scaffold along with a Running the app locally block containing the commands you need next.
