docs.title: iii. Reviewing the generated scaffold
docs.text:
Before moving on, spend a few minutes exploring the generated project in the Explorer. Pay attention to:

  • The finance-app/ folder layout — services, hooks, components, views
  • The mock data seam (VITE_USE_MOCK) that lets the app run offline
  • The company registry in constants/companies.ts (the single source of truth for tracked tickers)
  • The empty view components that Part 1 | Build's remaining steps will fill in
  • The test files already stubbed for the data layer and one rendering path

BEFORE YOU MOVE ON

You can continue to tinker with the scaffold if you wish — but be mindful that every prompt consumes tokens, and larger scaffolds tend to burn more than you'd expect. Your account's token budget will only reset monthly for IBMers, and trial accounts will expire once the budget is exhausted. Save exploration for after the core lab flow is complete.

Every file here traces back to a sub-task in the plan you just walked through. That traceability is what makes the codebase easy for Bob (and for you) to evolve in Part 2 | Evolve.

docs.title: iv. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Planning first, then scaffolding sub-task by sub-task, produces a codebase that matches intent (not just plausible boilerplate)
  • IBM Bob can turn a natural-language brief into a structured implementation plan with clear component and service boundaries
  • Sub-task sequencing makes the scope of each generation step explicit before code is written and gives the developer a clear approval gate at every stage
  • A mock-data seam lets the app run and be validated offline before any external integration is added
  • Local validation (lint + tests + build) belongs inside the scaffold plan as its own sub-task
  • Developers remain responsible for reviewing the plan, approving each sub-task, and validating the generated output

The next module builds on the scaffold. In 1-2 | Building and Validating the Dashboards, you will use Bob to integrate Yahoo Finance data, populate the three dashboard views, add validation, and prepare a review-ready commit for GitHub delivery.

docs.title: 1.2 Building and validating the dashboards
docs.text: PART 1 | BUILD

docs.title: i. Why this matters
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Building and Validating the Dashboards module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

The scaffold from the previous module runs, but it doesn't yet deliver any business value. The Current Day view renders mock quotes, and the Last 7 Days and Last Quarter tabs are empty.

Turning that scaffold into a real dashboard is where most of the engineering work actually lives. The data service has to fetch and normalize live market data. The views have to render summary cards and comparison charts across three time windows. And once the app is doing something real, it needs to survive the kinds of runtime failures that only surface when a live API is on the other end — missing tickers, environment-variable misreads, transient network errors.

AI MATURITY CURVE

Take note of two working patterns from the previous course as they reappear here. The screenshot-driven debugging pass is evidence-grounded delegation: Bob diagnoses against the failing UI and against the code on disk, exactly as you practiced in Module 2 | Delegate. And the closing diff review — together with the commit message and pull request description it produces — translates that same discipline into delivery form: the developer reads what changed, decides what it means, and approves what ships.

In this module, you will use IBM Bob to integrate the Yahoo Finance data layer, fill in the three dashboard views, optionally enable the live proxy, debug a real runtime error using a screenshot as evidence, and prepare a review-ready commit and pull request description for GitHub delivery.

Pay attention to how Bob operates in the middle of the loop — reading the existing scaffold, extending it deliberately, and diagnosing failures with the current file contents in hand rather than guessing.

docs.title: ii. Building and validating the dashboards
docs.text:
You will move through this module in four phases: data integration, dashboard views, optional live-data enablement, and a debug-and-review pass. Each phase builds on the previous one and stays inside the folder layout you approved in the plan.

  1. With Agent mode still active, ask Bob to implement the finance data layer. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar:

    Implement a finance data layer for IBM and its main competitors using Yahoo Finance data. Normalize the returned data so the UI can display quote summaries, short-term history, and quarterly trend views. Keep the code easy to extend if more companies need to be added later.

    Press the Send button to submit the task.

    Bob will extend the existing financeService, yahooAdapter, and mockData files, add new domain types for extended quote summaries and normalized history points, run the test suite, and confirm the lint and build gates are clean.

  1. With the data layer in place, ask Bob to build the three dashboard views. Copy and paste the following prompt:

    ` Build 2 to 3 dashboard views for the finance application: - current day market summary - last 7 days trend comparison - last quarter comparison view

    Include IBM and up to four competitors. Use charts and summary cards where appropriate. Keep the UI simple, readable, and demo-friendly. `

    Bob will fill in CurrentDayView, WeekView, and QuarterView — the IBM spotlight card, competitor grid, ranked performance bars, normalized line chart, and quarterly area chart with a sortable ranking table — then re-run validation.

    MODE SELECTION

    If a Carbon React mode is available in your Bob build, selecting it before submitting this prompt will tighten the visual result — the generated components inherit IBM Carbon Design System tokens and spacing rather than plain CSS.

  1. At this point, the app still runs entirely on deterministic mock fixtures. If you want to see the dashboard against real market data, Bob provides an optional two-terminal workflow. Otherwise, skip ahead to Step 8.

    The live-data path uses two terminals: one for the Yahoo Finance proxy, one for the dev server with mock mode turned off.

  1. Open a second terminal for the proxy. From the menu bar:

    Terminal → New Terminal

  1. In the new terminal, install the proxy dependencies and start it:

    cd finance-app
npm install yahoo-finance2 express
npm run proxy

    The Express proxy starts at http://127.0.0.1:3001 and forwards /api/finance/* calls to Yahoo Finance.

  1. Split the terminal so you can run the dev server side by side. Click the split icon in the terminal header, or from the dropdown next to the + button, choose Split Terminal.

  1. In the second pane, start the dev server with mock mode turned off:

    cd finance-app
VITE_USE_MOCK=false npm run dev

    Vite will forward /api/finance/* requests to the proxy. Reload the dashboard in your browser.

    PROXY MUST START FIRST

    The proxy must be listening on port 3001 before the dev server is started, or API calls will return 502 errors. If you see a retry banner in the app, the proxy is not reachable.

  1. This is where a real-world runtime failure shows up. When the dashboard loads against the live proxy, the Current Day view may render an error banner: Unable to load market summaries. Please try again.

    Rather than debugging this by hand, give the error to Bob. Take a screenshot of the browser, attach it to a new Bob task, and describe the issue in plain language.

  1. Attach the screenshot and enter a prompt like:

    I tried launching the application. It has an error. I attached the screenshot for your reference.

    Bob will inspect the screenshot, cross-reference the running code, and trace the error to the environment-variable check inside financeService.ts. Approve any commands Bob needs to run for diagnosis.

  1. Bob will apply the fix — flipping the mock-mode check from opt-in (=== 'true') to opt-out (!== 'false') so a missing or undefined value defaults to safe mock mode instead of accidentally hitting the network — update the tests, and re-run validation.

    A What was wrong and what's fixed summary appears in the sidebar, explaining the Vite client-side env-injection race that caused the runtime failure.

  1. Restart the dev server and reload the dashboard. The Current Day view now renders the IBM spotlight card, the four competitor cards with open/prev close/day range/52-week range/market cap/target fields, and matching live data.

    Click through the Last 7 Days and Last Quarter tabs to confirm the trend chart and area chart both render against live data.

  1. With the dashboards working, run one final validation pass to lock in test coverage and prepare the change for delivery. Copy and paste the following prompt:

    Add appropriate validation for the finance dashboard project. Create tests for the data transformation logic and at least one UI rendering path. Provide commands to run the application checks locally and summarize what success should look like.

    Bob will add missing unit and component tests, run the full lint/test/build gate, and confirm every gate is clean.

  1. Once validation is green, ask Bob to review the uncommitted diff and prepare the commit and pull request artifacts. Copy and paste:

    Review the uncommitted changes in this repository, summarize what was added for the finance dashboard, identify any missing pieces, and prepare a concise commit summary and pull request description for the initial application delivery.

    Bob will provide a change summary for every meaningful change, flag anything missing, and draft a commit message (plus a PR description.)

  1. Bob's PR description covers what shipped, how the data service is wired, how the mock/live seam works, and how to reproduce validation locally — everything a reviewer needs to approve the change.

    Copy the commit message and PR description — you'll paste them into GitHub at the start of Part 2 | Evolve.

docs.title: iii. Reviewing the completed build
docs.text:
Take a moment to review what Bob has produced end-to-end:

  • The data service normalizes Yahoo Finance responses into a stable domain model that the UI can rely on
  • The mock/live seam defaults to safe mock mode when the env var is missing or malformed
  • The three dashboard views cover current-day snapshots, 7-day comparative performance, and quarterly area trends with a sortable ranking table
  • The error path surfaces a clear retry banner instead of a crash when the proxy is unreachable
  • The test suite covers data-layer mapping, mock fixture integrity, normalization arithmetic, view rendering, and error states
  • The commit and PR description are ready to paste into GitHub as-is

Every layer remains extensible: adding a new company is a one-line change to the COMPANIES registry, and swapping the data source is contained to yahooAdapter.ts. That extensibility is what makes Part 2 possible.

docs.title: iv. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Integration and view work extend the scaffold while leaving its structure intact.
  • A mock/live seam that defaults to safe mode prevents accidental network calls in tests and dev.
  • Screenshots are a first-class debugging input for Bob — attaching a failing UI is often faster than describing it.
  • Test coverage belongs alongside the feature it validates, never deferred to a follow-up commit.
  • Bob-generated commit messages and PR descriptions should be reviewed but rarely need to be rewritten.
  • The reviewer artifact (PR description) is what Part 2 will iterate on — write it once, well.

The next module hands the codebase over to GitHub. In Part 2 | Evolve, you will push this branch to a real repository, open an issue for a new feature, and let Bob take the request all the way to a merge-ready pull request.

docs.title: 2.1 Publishing to GitHub
docs.text: PART 2 | EVOLVE

docs.title: i. Why this matters
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Publishing to GitHub module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

The finance dashboard from Part 1 | Build runs, passes its validation gates, and is ready to share. But it still lives only inside your IDE workspace. In fact, the workspace is not yet even a git repository — initialization has never occurred, not a single commit exists, and no .gitignore is present to keep dependencies and build artifacts out of version control. Until the code reaches a shared repository, there is no collaborative workspace for issues to capture requirements, for pull requests to carry review, or for continuous integration (CI) to guard the main branch.

Modern delivery treats GitHub as that workspace. An issue is opened, a branch is created, code is written, tests run, a pull request is reviewed, and something is merged. Part 2 of this hands-on lab places IBM Bob inside that loop. Before Bob can fetch an issue or prepare a pull request, however, the repository has to exist in two places: locally as an initialized git repository, and on GitHub.com as the shared remote.

PUBLISH TO YOUR OWN GITHUB REPOSITORIES

A personal GitHub.com account is required for this module and the rest of Part 2 | Evolve.

If your personal GitHub account is already linked to the IBM GitHub enterprise account, you can still publish code to repositories under your own (personal) account. However, you will encounter restrictions on what you can commit and publish to the IBM GitHub repositories — as only approved contributors are able to commit to such endpoints.

To publish code for the purposes of Part 2 | Evolve, you will need to ensure that code is committed via your personal repositories, not the IBM repositories. The repository can be public or private. Bob's workflow is identical either way.

In this module, you will:

  • Create the GitHub repository, so the remote exists before anything is pushed to it
  • Let Bob inspect the workspace and surface anything blocking a clean push
  • Initialize the local repository, putting the Part 1 code under version control
  • Publish the code, using the commands Bob prepares
  • Enable the collaboration features the rest of Part 2 depends on
  • Open the issue that drives the next enhancement

Pay attention to how Bob participates even in this administrative phase. It inspects the working tree, catches blockers like a missing .gitignore, and prepares the exact commands, while you retain control of the actual push.

AI MATURITY CURVE

This module applies the Scale & Extend stage of the AI Maturity Curve to the delivery platform itself. Bob's reach now extends beyond the IDE — inspecting the working tree, surfacing blockers, and preparing the exact commands — while the one action that publishes the work, the push, remains yours to perform. As you learned throughout the previous course, extending an agent's reach and retaining control over consequential actions are practiced together, and this chapter asks you to do exactly that.

docs.title: ii. Publishing to GitHub
docs.text:
You will move through this module in four phases, in this order:

  1. Create the empty repository on GitHub.com (steps 1 and 2), so the remote URL exists before anything else.
  2. Let Bob check readiness and produce the delivery artifacts (steps 3 and 4).
  3. Initialize the local repository and push (steps 5 through 7).
  4. Verify and stage the collaboration surface (steps 8 through 10): confirm the publish, enable Issues, create the feature branch, and open the enhancement issue the next module builds on.

  1. Create the repository on GitHub first, so you have a remote URL to push to later. In your browser, go to GitHub and click New next to Top repositories on the dashboard, or navigate directly to https://github.com/new.

    On the Create a new repository form, click the Repository name field and enter finance-app (or your preferred name).

    In the Description field, paste IBM Bob Workshop Finance Dashboard Application.

    Under Configuration, select a visibility. Public or Private is your choice; Private was used here.

    Confirm Add README is toggled Off, and leave Add .gitignore on No .gitignore and Add license on No license. The repository must stay empty because you are pushing existing code. Then click Create repository.

  1. GitHub will land on the Quick setup page showing the repository's remote URL, in the form https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/finance-app.git

    Copy and store it within a notepad for now, as you will later need to paste it into a git command in Step 6.

  1. Now let Bob assess the workspace. Back in the Bob IDE, with Agent mode active, copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar:

    Inspect the current repository changes, summarize the current implementation status of the finance dashboard, and identify whether the project is ready to be committed and pushed to GitHub.

    Hit Enter or press the Send button to submit the task.

    Bob will begin calling tools to inspect the repository, and will pause for approval before the first one. The command it proposes is read-only, a look at recent history such as git log --oneline -10. Click Approve once to let it run.

    Bob works through the Todo List pinned at the top of the session as it inspects. This is the same validation Todo List Bob completed at the end of Part 1 | Build, now showing 6/6 with every item green, and it is the baseline Bob is assessing for delivery readiness:

    TASK OBJECTIVES Sub-Task 1 Fix the dev:mock script environment variable (USE_MOCK → VITE_USE_MOCK) and add the validate and test:coverage scripts Sub-Task 2 Extend formatters.test.js with formatVolume, formatIndex, and formatAxisDate suites Sub-Task 3 Add PerformanceBadge.test.jsx covering rendering and the positive, negative, and null states Sub-Task 4 Add RankingStrip.test.jsx covering sort order, all symbols rendered, null-percentage safety, and price display Sub-Task 5 Add WeekChangeSummary.test.jsx covering the chip per symbol, start and end prices, and the empty guard Sub-Task 6 Run the full validation suite and confirm all checks pass

    Bob reruns the validation suite against the code on disk, explores the source folders, then checks what git would exclude. It finds no root-level .gitignore, meaning node_modules/, dist/, and .DS_Store would all be committed, and may try to create the file itself.

    Rather than approving each remaining inspection command one at a time, click Approve for task so Bob can finish the assessment without stopping at every read-only command.

    IF BOB CANNOT WRITE THE .gitignore

    Bob may report Failed to write file .gitignore because the workspace's own protection blocks writes to a root-level gitignore. This is not a problem. Step 5 below creates the file from the terminal instead.

    Bob will inspect the workspace and report two kinds of findings:

    • Code readiness: Bob reruns the validation gates and reports the results, for example npm run lint with zero errors, the full test suite passing, and a clean build.
    • Delivery blockers: expect Bob to point out that the workspace is not yet a git repository (commands like git status return fatal: not a git repository) and that no .gitignore exists, which means node_modules/ (thousands of files) and dist/ would be committed. This is normal. Part 1 never initialized version control, and steps 5 through 7 below fix both findings.

    When the assessment finishes, Bob produces the delivery artifact: a numbered, copy-paste sequence of the exact git commands for the push, ending with a staging check, the commit, and the push itself.

    Read the tail of that artifact carefully, because the next steps reuse it:

    • A staging check (git status and git diff --staged --stat) with an explicit reminder that node_modules and dist must not appear in the staged set
    • A commit message in conventional-commit form, for example feat: add initial React finance dashboard application, with a body covering the five tracked companies, the three time-window views, the data layer, the passing test count, and the CI workflow
    • The push command, git push -u origin <branch>
    • A closing note that once the push lands, the CI workflow under .github/workflows/ runs automatically: it installs dependencies, lints, runs the test suite with VITE_USE_MOCK=true, builds, and uploads dist/ as a workflow artifact

  1. Ask Bob for the delivery artifacts you will use during the push and later on GitHub. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar, then hit Enter to execute the instructions:

    Generate a concise summary of the finance dashboard implementation, propose a commit message, and prepare a pull request description that explains the new application, dashboards, and validation steps.

    Bob will pause for approval before its first tool call. The command is read-only, a find over finance-app/src that lists the source files so the summary is grounded in what is actually on disk. Click Approve once.

    Bob reruns the validation chain, reports Live validation confirmed, and produces the three deliverables as a single self-contained HTML report, the same way it produced the implementation plan in Part 1. Alongside the report, Bob posts a plain-text summary in the sidebar so you can read the essentials without opening anything.

    The sidebar summary describes what was built in one paragraph, then quantifies it under By the numbers: 47 source files in src/, 2 server files, 2 GitHub delivery artifacts, 114 tests passing across 7 suites (75 unit plus 39 component render), a production build producing 7 split chunks, and npm run validate exiting 0.

    It then tells you where each artifact goes, which is the part that matters for the rest of this module:

    ARTIFACT WHERE IT GOES Commit message (section 2) Into git commit -m "...". The full multi-line body is already formatted for a standard git commit PR description (section 3) Pasted into the GitHub PR body when the pull request is opened from feature/initial-finance-dashboard into main

    Bob also notes that once the branch is pushed, the CI workflow at .github/workflows/finance-app-ci.yml runs the identical lint → test → build chain and uploads the dist/ folder as a downloadable artifact for reviewers.

    Now click Open on the Finance Dashboard — Commit & PR Package card to review the full report in the IDE. The report is written to a temporary bob-artifacts/ directory, so open it before starting a new task.

    The report opens with a Validation live run panel confirming the three gates Bob just executed against the code on disk: lint reporting 0 errors and 0 warnings, every test in the suite passing, and a clean production build with no warnings. Below the panel, the report is organized into numbered sections.

    • 1 · Implementation summary: what the finance-app/ directory delivers — a complete React 18 market analytics dashboard tracking IBM against Microsoft, Oracle, SAP, and Salesforce, with a lightweight Express proxy isolating the browser from third-party API concerns and an offline mock mode (VITE_USE_MOCK=true) that lets the full UI run with no network access, used by the dev server, the tests, and CI.
    • Three views: a table mapping each time window to what it shows and the components that render it — Today (RankingStrip, SummaryCard), Last 7 Days (LineChart, WeekChangeSummary), and Last Quarter (AreaChart in base-100 index mode, so IBM at ~$175 and MSFT at ~$415 sit on the same Y axis).
    • Source file inventory: a layer-by-layer table of config, constants, utilities, data service, state, components, and tests, naming the files in each layer and the responsibility it carries.
    • 2 · Commit message and 3 · Pull request description: the two artifacts you carry forward.

    YOUR NUMBERS WILL DIFFER

    Those three green results are the substance of the report. The run shown here reports 114 tests across 7 suites, but the exact counts and timings depend on what Part 1 | Build produced on your machine and are not something to match.

    Keep both artifacts handy: the commit message is used in Step 7, and the PR description is used when a pull request is opened on GitHub.

  1. Time to fix the blockers Bob found. Open a new Terminal in the IDE (Terminal → New Terminal) and create the .gitignore at the workspace root, so dependencies and build artifacts never enter version control:

    cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
node_modules/
dist/
.DS_Store
.env
coverage/
EOF

  1. You will next need to execute the complete code block after making modifications.

    • Copy and paste the code block below to a notepad for editing
    • Retrieve the GitHub repository remote URL that you recorded earlier in Step 1
    • Substitute the <REMOTE_URL> placeholder token with your repository remote URL
    • Copy and paste the modified code block into the Terminal console and press Enter to execute
    # Initialize the repository
git init

# Connect the GitHub remote
git remote add origin <REMOTE_URL>

# Verify the remote was added
git remote -v

  1. Stage, commit, name the default branch, and finally push it. Use the commit message Bob proposed in Step 4.

    • Copy and paste the code block below to a notepad for editing
    • Retrieve the commit message that IBM Bob recommended earlier in Step 4
    • Substitute the <COMMIT_MESSAGE> placeholder token with the message from Step 4
    • Copy and paste the modified code block into the Terminal console and press Enter to execute
    # Stage everything
git add .

# IMPORTANT: confirm node_modules and dist do NOT appear in the staged list
git status

# Commit using the message Bob proposed
git commit -m "<COMMIT_MESSAGE>"

# Name the default branch main
git branch -M main

# Push to GitHub
git push -u origin main

    The commit output lists every file as create mode 100644 ..., so read it and confirm that only source files are being tracked. The push output then reports the objects written and ends with the two lines that confirm the publish succeeded:

    * [new branch]      main -> main
Branch 'main' set up to track remote branch 'main' from 'origin'.

    RENAME THE BRANCH AFTER THE FIRST COMMIT

    git branch -M main renames the branch you are currently on. Immediately after git init there are no commits yet, so that branch does not exist as a reference and the rename fails with error: refname refs/heads/master not found. Git 2.30 and later handle this case, but older versions do not, so this workshop renames the branch after the commit. This is also the order GitHub's own Quick setup page uses.

    If you have already hit the error, either commit first and then rerun git branch -M main, or point HEAD at the branch directly with git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/main.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: AUTHENTICATION ISSUES

    GitHub no longer accepts account passwords over HTTPS. If the push prompts for credentials, use a Personal Access Token (PAT) in place of the password, or configure SSH keys and use the SSH remote URL instead. See GitHub's authentication documentation for both paths.

    If the push is rejected, confirm you have write access to the repository, check that no branch protection rule is blocking the push, and verify the remote URL with git remote -v.

  1. Verify the published repository in your browser. Refresh the repository page on GitHub.com and confirm:

    • All files from Part 1 are visible: the application source, the docs, and the PR template
    • node_modules/ and dist/ are not in the file tree
    • The Finance App CI workflow is listed under the Actions tab
    • The pull request template is visible at .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md

    Open the repository from your GitHub dashboard.

    • The repository home page should show a single commit carrying Bob's commit message, on one branch, with the root file tree: .github/, docs/, finance-app/, .gitignore, LICENSE, README.md, and the workshop markdown files.
    • Confirm that node_modules/ and dist/ are not included within that list (the .gitignore you created in Step 5 is what kept them out)

    Click into finance-app/ and check the application directory the same way. You should see public/, server/, src/, and the config files (.eslintrc.cjs, index.html, package.json, package-lock.json, vite.config.js), with no node_modules/ and no dist/.

    Note that package-lock.json is committed, which is what lets CI run a reproducible npm ci.

    NO WORKFLOW RUNS YET — AND THAT IS EXPECTED

    The Actions tab will list Finance App CI in the left sidebar but report There are no workflow runs yet. GitHub detects the workflow by parsing .github/workflows/finance-app-ci.yml on the default branch; detecting it is not the same as running it.

    The workflow is deliberately scoped to the delivery paths that matter, and a direct push to main is not one of them:

    on:
  push:
    branches:
      - 'feature/**'
      - 'fix/**'
      - 'chore/**'
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

    The first run arrives in Step 9, when the feature/initial-finance-dashboard branch is pushed and matches feature/**.

    Then go to Settings → General and scroll to the Features section. - Confirm the Issues checkbox is ticked, since the feature request workflow in the next module depends on it. - Leave Issue permissions on the default, Creation allowed by: All users.

  1. Create the feature branch for the workshop. Feature work never lands on main directly; it travels on its own branch and arrives through a pull request. Back in the IDE terminal:

    # Create and switch to a new feature branch
git checkout -b feature/initial-finance-dashboard

# Push the branch to GitHub
git push -u origin feature/initial-finance-dashboard

    The terminal confirms the switch with Switched to a new branch 'feature/initial-finance-dashboard'. At that point the branch exists only locally; the git push that follows is what publishes it.

    This push is what starts CI. The branch name matches the feature/** pattern in the workflow trigger, so return to the repository on GitHub and click the Actions tab. The repository header should now read 2 Branches.

    Where the Actions tab reported no runs in Step 8, it now shows 1 workflow run, titled with your commit message and labelled Finance App CI #1, with the commit hash, your username, and the feature/initial-finance-dashboard branch it ran against.

    Click the run to open it.

    The run summary is what this entire module has been building toward. Confirm:

    • Triggered via push on feature/initial-finance-dashboard, with Status: Success
    • The single Lint → Test → Build job carrying a green check, completing in well under a minute
    • Artifacts: 1, listing finance-app-dist, the built dist/ folder uploaded by the workflow's final step and downloadable by any reviewer

    The same gates Bob ran locally in Step 3 and Step 4 have now run on a clean machine, against the code as GitHub received it. That is the point of pushing to a branch first: the validation is no longer taking your word for it.

    AN ANNOTATION WARNING IS NOT A FAILURE

    The run may show Annotations: 1 warning reporting that Node.js 20 is deprecated and that actions/checkout, actions/setup-node, and actions/upload-artifact are being forced onto a newer Node.js runtime. This is GitHub deprecating the runtime its own actions run on rather than a problem with the finance dashboard. The job status is still Success, and the workshop continues unchanged.

    BRANCH NAMING CONVENTIONS

    A consistent branch naming convention keeps AI assisted work traceable alongside human work. This workshop uses the pattern most teams will recognize:

    • feature/initial-finance-dashboard (created just now, the published baseline)
    • feature/user-selected-company-chart (created in the next module, carries the enhancement)
    • fix/chart-data-normalization (the shape a future bug fix would take)

  1. Finally, open the issue that drives the next module. Click the Issues tab in the repository header, then click New issue.

    On the Create new issue form, fill in:

    • Add a title: Add a graph for a user selected company
    • Add a description:
    Add a new graph based on a company indicated by the user.

* Allow the dashboard to accept a stock symbol or company selection
* Render an additional comparison chart for the selected company
* Invalid or unsupported symbols should produce a clear message to the user
* The existing dashboards for IBM and its competitors must remain unchanged
    WHY IS THE BODY WRITTEN THIS WAY?

    The description is deliberately written as an outcome plus four constraints rather than as a set of implementation instructions. It says what the user should be able to do, what must appear, how failure should behave, and what must not regress. That is enough for Bob to plan against, and it leaves the design decisions where they belong. Notice that the last bullet is a guard: it tells Bob what success must not break.

    • Leave Assignees, Labels, Projects, and Milestone empty (Bob reads the title and body, and nothing else here changes what it does in the next module)
    • When ready to continue, click Create

    Note the issue number GitHub assigns (typically #1). Bob will fetch this issue by number in the next module.

docs.title: iii. Verification checklist
docs.text:
Before moving on, confirm every row. The next two modules assume all of this is in place:

CHECK WHAT TO CONFIRM GitHub repository created and accessible Repository page loads at github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/finance-app .gitignore in place node_modules/ and dist/ absent from the GitHub file tree Local git repository initialized git status reports a branch, not an error Local repository connected to the GitHub remote git remote -v shows origin Code pushed to GitHub successfully Part 1 Build files visible on the main branch CI workflow detected Actions tab lists Finance App CI, with no runs until the feature branch is pushed Issues and Pull Requests enabled Settings → General → Features Feature branch created and pushed feature/initial-finance-dashboard visible on GitHub CI run green Actions shows a passing Finance App CI run for the feature branch Enhancement issue created Issue #1 open in the Issues tab

docs.title: iv. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Publishing happens in a fixed order: create the empty GitHub repository, let Bob confirm readiness, initialize the local repository, then push. Each step depends on the one before it.
  • Bob catches delivery blockers a developer might miss, like a missing .gitignore that would commit thousands of dependency files, and prepares the exact commands to fix them.
  • The developer performs the push. Bob prepares the delivery, but the repository remains under your control.
  • Feature work travels on branches, never directly on main. The baseline branch exists now, and the enhancement gets its own branch in the next module.
  • An issue is the entry point of the evolution loop. The next module starts from issue #1 rather than from a prompt written from scratch.

The next module is the central demonstration of the lab. In Implementing a Feature Request, Bob will fetch the issue you just created, analyze the requested scope, implement the new company chart, and validate the result.

docs.title: 2.2 Implementing a feature request
docs.text: PART 2 | EVOLVE

docs.title: i. Why this matters
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Implementing a Feature Request module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

This module is the central demonstration of the lab. All of your work prior to this stage— the plan, the scaffold, the dashboards, the push to GitHub —has been preparation for the next steps. Now a real enhancement request exists as a GitHub issue, and the question that this hands-on lab originally posed will be answered: can IBM Bob take a repository enhancement request and convert it into working, validated implementation?

In this module, you will use IBM Bob to fetch and analyze the GitHub issue from the previous module, define the acceptance criteria, identify the required UI, state, and data service changes, implement the chart for a company selected by the user, and validate the result, all without disturbing the existing dashboards for IBM and its competitors.

The enhancement request stays fixed throughout this module: users can enter or select a company or ticker, the app resolves data for it, a new graph renders alongside the existing dashboards, and invalid symbols produce a clear message to the user.

Pay attention to how Bob grounds each phase in repository context (the issue text, the existing service layer, the company registry) rather than generating an isolated feature in a vacuum.

AI MATURITY CURVE

The requirements gate ahead is the plan-approval discipline of Module 2 | Delegate, now applied to work that arrives from outside the conversation. A four-bullet GitHub issue goes in; numbered acceptance criteria — each with its verification method attached — come out, and nothing is implemented until you agree to the scope. The pattern is unchanged from the first time you practiced it: your judgment governs the branch points, and Bob works autonomously between them.

docs.title: ii. Implementing a feature request
docs.text:
You will progress through this module via five actions: create the branch the enhancement will travel on, ask Bob to analyze the requested scope and approve it at the requirements gate, ask Bob to implement the enhancement and approve its subtasks, run the validation gate, and verify the result in the browser. This mirrors the arc of a real delivery cycle, from requirements through development to testing, compressed into a single working session.

  1. Every enhancement gets its own branch. Open a new Terminal (Ctrl+Shift+`) within the Bob IDE and create the branch this feature will travel on, following the naming convention from the previous module:

    # Create and switch to the enhancement branch
git checkout -b feature/user-selected-company-chart

# Push the branch to GitHub so it exists on the remote
git push -u origin feature/user-selected-company-chart

    Confirm with git branch that feature/user-selected-company-chart is now the active branch. All of the implementation work in this module lands here, never on main.

  1. With Agent mode active, ask Bob to fetch and analyze the enhancement request.

    • Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar:
    Fetch the GitHub issue or pull request context requesting a new graph driven by a company selected by the user. Analyze the requested enhancement, define the likely acceptance criteria, identify the required UI, state, and data service changes, and explain how to implement the feature without breaking the existing dashboards that compare IBM against its competitors.
    • Press Send (or hit Enter) to have Bob begin grounding the analysis in real code
    • Bob will pause for approval before its first tool call, such as a read-only listing like find finance-app/src -type f | sort
    • Click Approve once
    • Bob resolves the request from repository context, restates it in engineering terms, and produces a Todo List that plans the work end to end
    SUB-TASK OBJECTIVES Sub-Task 1 Add customSymbol and setCustomSymbol to dashboardStore Sub-Task 2 Add a useCustomSymbolData hook to useMarketData Sub-Task 3 Build the CompanySelector component and its CSS module Sub-Task 4 Build the CustomSymbolPanel component and its CSS module Sub-Task 5 Wire CompanySelector and CustomSymbolPanel into the dashboard page Sub-Task 6 Write tests for the store, the selector, and the panel Sub-Task 7 Add a mock data entry for the custom symbol, for example NVDA Sub-Task 8 Run npm run validate and confirm zero warnings with every test passing

    Alongside the plan, Bob delivers the analysis itself as a report: Feature Request Analysis — User-Selected Company Graph

    • Click Open to read it
    • Notice that the issue asked for four things and Bob derived nine, each with a verification method attached
    • Scroll to the end of Bob's response for the impact map and the non-breaking guarantee

    This report is the requirements gate. It plays the same role the implementation plan played in Part 1: scope is agreed before a line of code is written. The report is tagged Enhancement and Non-breaking, names the branch it targets, restates the business request, and then does the thing that matters most, turning a four-bullet issue into numbered acceptance criteria that each say how they will be proven:

    ID CRITERION VERIFIABLE BY AC-1 A text input accepts any 1–5 letter uppercase ticker symbol Integration test, valid input calls onSubmit AC-2 The input is validated before fetch; empty or non-alpha strings show an inline error Integration test, submitting empty or IBM1 shows an alert AC-3 While data is loading a spinner is shown inside the new panel Integration test, mock returns isLoading: true AC-4 If the symbol is unknown or the fetch fails, a clear error message is shown Integration test, mock returns isError: true or quote: null AC-5 On success a price chart and summary card render for the selected symbol Integration test, panel renders with fixture data AC-6 The three existing views remain untouched All 114 existing tests continue to pass AC-7 Clearing the selection hides the chart panel Integration test, Clear button calls onClear AC-8 The selected symbol persists across time-window tab switches Store unit test, customSymbol survives setActiveWindow AC-9 In mock mode the panel works offline with a fixture ticker Mock fixture added to quotes.json and history.json

    BOB STOPS AND WAITS

    Bob ends the analysis by naming the next step and holding: the implementation subtasks are planned but not started. Nothing is written until you ask in Step 3. The requirements gate functions as a genuine checkpoint such that nothing advances until you say so.

    ISSUE COVERAGE REVIEW

    If your Bob build exposes slash commands, /review --issue-coverage performs a related workflow from the review side. It checks whether the changes on a branch actually cover what a referenced issue asked for. It is a useful cross check at the end of this module once the implementation exists.

    Bob lists exactly which files change and, just as importantly, which do not: zero changes to the API layer, the data normalization service, the company registry, the existing chart components, or the Express proxy. The new state is a new field on the store, the new data path uses its own React Query cache keys so it cannot collide with the existing ones, and the new panel only mounts once the user has entered a symbol, so it is invisible until it is asked for.

    If anything in the analysis contradicts the issue, say so in the sidebar and let Bob revise before you move on. Correcting scope here costs one message; correcting it after implementation costs a rewrite.

  1. With the scope agreed, ask Bob to implement the enhancement. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar:

    Implement the requested feature so that the finance dashboard allows a user to indicate a company symbol and see a new graph for that company. Reuse the existing finance data layer where possible, keep the UX simple, and preserve the existing dashboards. If a symbol has no data available, show a clear no-data message rather than falling back to another company's data.
    • Press Send (or hit Enter) to execute.
    • Bob starts the subtasks planned in Step 2 and asks for approval as it goes
    • The Todo List at the top of the session tracks progress
    • The header will read All tasks completed once Bob is done

    Watch the order in which Bob writes. Rather than creating files one at a time, it groups them into dependency-ordered batches, so nothing is written before the things it imports exist:

    BATCH WHAT IT WRITES Batch 1 The store change: customSymbol and setCustomSymbol added to dashboardStore.js Batch 2 The data hook: useCustomSymbolData() exported from useMarketData.js Batch 3 The new components: CompanySelector and CustomSymbolPanel, each with its CSS module Batch 4 The wiring: CompanySelector and CustomSymbolPanel mounted in DashboardPage.jsx, below the existing view switch Batch 5 The fixtures and tests: an NVDA entry appended to the mock JSON, plus the new test files

    Each batch reports the files it touched. None of the existing view components are rewritten to make room for the new panel.

    After the last batch, Bob posts a What was built summary.

    Step 4 breaks the test count into new versus pre-existing and turns it into a formal verdict.

    Below the numbers, Bob lists the work by layer. These are the rows that carry the enhancement:

    LAYER FILES NOTES Store dashboardStore.js customSymbol + setCustomSymbol for the new feature Hooks useMarketData.js, useCompanies.js useCustomSymbolData() is the new hook Dashboard DashboardPage.jsx + existing views CompanySelector + CustomSymbolPanel wired below existing views New feature CompanySelector.jsx, CustomSymbolPanel.jsx Pure and props-driven; validates the ticker with /^[A-Z]{1,5}$/ Services financeData.js, financeApi.js, quotes.json, history.json NVDA fixture included Tests 10 files, 3 unit and 7 integration dashboardStore.test.js, CompanySelector.test.jsx, and CustomSymbolPanel.test.jsx cover the feature

    Every one of those rows was named in the impact map in Step 2, and nothing turned up that the analysis did not predict. The API client, the normalization service, the company registry, and the existing chart components have no feature changes.

    The summary ends with a Feature behaviour paragraph. This is what you will check in the browser in Step 5:

    Enter any ticker (for example NVDA) in the Custom Company Chart section and it appears permanently below the Today / 7 Days / Quarter views. The panel shows a quote summary card plus a 30-day line chart. Invalid input is rejected before any fetch. Clear removes the panel. Under npm run dev:mock, NVDA resolves from the fixture, and any other symbol returns the No data found state.

    Remember the last sentence for Step 5. In mock mode, only NVDA returns data. Every other symbol shows No data found, whether it is a real company like AAPL or a made-up ticker like ZZZZ.

    Bob stops here without committing anything. The counter at the bottom of the sidebar shows how many files changed. Do not commit or undo them: Step 4 runs the validation against these changes, and the next module reviews the diff before anything is committed.

    ATTENTION: YOUR RESULTS MAY VARY

    As in Part 1 | Build, Bob's implementation is not deterministic. The exact subtasks, file names, test counts, and UX shape (input field versus dropdown, panel placement) may differ from what is shown here. Judge the result against the acceptance criteria rather than against these screenshots.

    The session shown here rebuilt the whole application before adding the feature, which is why it reports 62 files changed. If you carried your Part 1 code forward, expect far fewer.

  1. With the implementation in place, run the validation gate. Copy and paste the following prompt:

    Run the appropriate project validation for the new graph feature for a company selected by the user. Summarize what passed, what failed, and whether the branch is ready to push back to GitHub.

    Press Send (or hit Enter). Bob runs the lint, test, and build gates against the code on disk, fixes anything that fails, and reports whether the branch is ready to deliver. If a gate fails, let Bob work through it.

    When it finishes, Bob answers with Validation result: PASS, branch is ready, then shows the results behind that verdict.

    Gate results lists the three checks Bob ran. These are the same three GitHub Actions will run on the branch once it is pushed:

    CHECK RESULT WHAT IT MEANS ESLint 0 errors, 0 warnings No code-style or correctness warnings anywhere in src/ Vitest 128 / 128 passed Every test in all 10 suites passed, 0 failures Vite build Clean The production build compiled with no warnings

    Bob then lists what the 30 new tests actually check, one row per test file:

    SUITE TESTS SCENARIOS dashboardStore.test.js 12 Initial customSymbol: '', setCustomSymbol uppercases and trims, replaces a previous value, clears back to '', and survives setActiveWindow CompanySelector.test.jsx 12 Render, valid submit calls onSubmit('NVDA'), draft clears after submit, empty submit shows the error alert, digits rejected, Clear button visibility, onClear callback, active-symbol label, error clears on keystroke CustomSymbolPanel.test.jsx 6 Loading spinner, fetch-error banner, no-quote banner, success panel renders, ticker in header, empty-history fallback

    Those scenarios match the acceptance criteria from Step 2: digits rejected and empty submit are AC-2, the loading spinner is AC-3, the error banners are AC-4, the success panel is AC-5, the Clear button is AC-7, and survives setActiveWindow is AC-8.

    Zero regressions answers AC-6:

    All 98 pre-existing tests pass without modification. The store change adds new fields only; the DashboardPage.jsx change appends the feature section after the existing view switch, so no existing JSX was removed or reordered.

    Bob ends with the commands to deliver the branch: git add -A and a commit whose message lists the store field, the hook, the two components, the NVDA fixture, the ResizeObserver polyfill, and the 30 new tests.

    DO NOT RUN THE PUSH COMMANDS YET

    The branch is ready, but do not commit or push yet. The next module has Bob review the diff first, then prepares the delivery commands with the pull request in mind. Review the commands here; the next module is where you will run them.

    IF A GATE COMES BACK RED

    A first-run failure is normal and is worth watching rather than skipping past. The ResizeObserver polyfill in the run above exists because the chart component needs a browser API that jsdom does not implement, which surfaces as a failing test before it becomes a one-line fix in the test setup. Tell Bob to fix what failed and rerun the validation. The branch is not ready until this response reads PASS with all three gates green.

  1. Verify the feature in the running application. Everything up to this point has been Bob reporting on its own work. This is where you check it yourself.

    With an open Terminal console, start the dev server in mock mode with the following commands:

    cd finance-app
npm run dev:mock

    Copy the local URL Vite prints, http://localhost:5173/, into a browser. The dashboard loads on the Today view with a MOCK badge beside the title, confirming everything on screen is fixture data.

    Check the original dashboard before touching the new feature. The Today / Last 7 Days / Last Quarter switch is still in the header, Daily Performance Ranking still ranks the tracked companies with their bars and daily percentages, and Quote Detail still renders a card per company. Nothing from Part 1 was moved or restyled to make room for the enhancement.

    SIX COMPANIES, NOT FIVE

    The ranking and quote grid above list six companies rather than the original five, because the NVDA fixture Bob added in Step 3 was also registered in companies.js, the single source of truth for the tracked set. That is an additive entry in the registry rather than a change to the views, and it is why NVDA behaves like a first-class company here. Your run may show the original five with NVDA available only to the custom panel. Either is acceptable.

    Now scroll to the bottom of the page. Below Quote Detail there is a new Custom Company section holding the Custom Company Chart panel: one line of instruction, a ticker input, and a Load button. This is CompanySelector, mounted after the existing view switch exactly as the impact map in Step 2 promised.

    Start with a malformed entry. Type IBM1 and click Load.

    The input rejects it inline with Ticker must be 1–5 letters (e.g. NVDA) and no fetch is issued. That is AC-2 confirmed in the browser, and it is the same rule the digits-rejected case in CompanySelector.test.jsx exercises. An empty submission behaves the same way.

    Next, try a valid ticker that has no data in mock mode, such as AAPL.

    The panel accepts the symbol, reports Currently showing: AAPL, and replaces the chart with a clear message: No data found for symbol "AAPL". Check the ticker and try again. That is AC-4: a valid symbol the app cannot resolve produces a clear message instead of a crash or an empty chart.

    Finally, load NVDA. The panel shows NVIDIA's quote card and its 30-day price chart. Click Clear and the panel disappears. Load it again, then switch between Today, Last 7 Days, and Last Quarter: the panel stays put.

docs.title: iii. Reviewing the enhancement
docs.text:
Walk the acceptance criteria one final time against what is now running:

ACCEPTANCE CRITERION HOW IT IS MET Users can enter or select a company or ticker New selector control on the dashboard The app fetches or resolves data for that company Data service extended to resolve arbitrary tickers, reusing the Part 1 Build layer A new graph is rendered without removing the existing dashboards Additive chart panel; the Current Day, Last 7 Days, and Last Quarter views unchanged Invalid symbols produce a clear message to the user Malformed input is rejected inline before any fetch; a valid symbol with no data shows a clear no-data message Tests or validation steps cover the new behavior New unit and component tests; the full lint, test, and build gate is green

A GitHub issue went in, and a working, tested feature came out, with the analysis, the plan, and the test results visible at every step.

docs.title: iv. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• A GitHub issue is enough context for Bob to derive acceptance criteria, work out which files are affected, and identify what must not break.
  • Agreeing the scope before any code is written is the same checkpoint the plan review provided in Part 1 | Build.
  • Reusing the existing data layer keeps the enhancement additive: nothing was rewritten or restructured to fit it in.
  • The branch is not done until lint, tests, and build all pass, and the feature has been checked in the browser.
  • Bob is not deterministic, so your component and file names may differ from the screenshots. Judge your result against the acceptance criteria.

Don't commit any code yet. In the final module, Preparing the Pull Request, Bob reviews the diff, writes the pull request description, prepares the push, and hands the enhancement off for merge.

docs.title: 2.3 Preparing a pull request
docs.text: PART 2 | EVOLVE

docs.title: i. Why this matters
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Preparing a Pull Request module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

A convincing agentic workflow must show how the work gets finished— reviewed, described, delivered, and merged —every bit of detail as how the code gets written. The chart for a company selected by the user now runs locally and passes validation. From GitHub's perspective, however, nothing has happened yet. The issue is still open, the feature branch has no new commits, and no reviewer has anything to look at.

The realistic closure path takes one of three shapes: Bob updates the PR branch with the requested code and tests, Bob prepares the branch and PR notes for a maintainer to merge, or a downstream GitHub automation merges or closes the PR after validation. This module demonstrates the maintainer merge path, the most common in practice.

In this module, you will use IBM Bob to review the updated branch, generate the pull request description, prepare the push commands, open the pull request on GitHub, and close the loop by merging the enhancement and letting GitHub close the issue that started it.

Note how the work is split: Bob prepares everything, GitHub runs the checks, and a person makes the decision to merge.

AI MATURITY CURVE

Take note of where this final module places the authority to act. Bob prepares the review, the description, and the commands; GitHub's CI re-validates the work on a machine no agent can edit; and the decision to merge — the single action that changes main — belongs to a person. The control discipline that has run through this entire curriculum concludes precisely where it matters most: at the moment of delivery.

docs.title: ii. Preparing a pull request
docs.text:
You will progress through this module across three phases: review and describe the change, push and open the pull request, and merge to close the loop.

  1. With Agent mode active, ask Bob to review the branch and prepare everything needed to deliver it. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar:

    Review the updated branch, summarize the feature implementation, generate a pull request update description, and provide the git commands needed to push the changes so the GitHub pull request can be completed.
    • Press Send (or hit Enter)
    • Bob asks for approval before its first command
    • It is read-only: git log, git status, and git diff --stat, run in finance-app to see the current state of the branch
    • Click Approve once

    Bob reads through the changes you have not committed yet and produces a report titled feat: add user-selected company chart. Click Open to read it.

    The header shows where the change is going, Base: main ← Head: feature/user-selected-company-chart, along with status badges for the checks, the test count, and the number of new files. The Closes #1 tag links the work back to the issue. Below the header, the report is structured like a pull request body:

    • Feature summary: what the new section does. It sits below the existing dashboards, the user types a ticker, and a quote card and 30-day line chart render for it. The three original views are untouched. The summary also covers input validation before any network call, loading and error states, the Clear button, the symbol surviving tab switches, and the NVDA fixture that lets the feature run offline.
    • New data flow: a diagram following one submission from the input to the data layer, CompanySelector → dashboardStore → DashboardPage → CustomSymbolPanel → useCustomSymbolData → financeApi / mock. One line underneath explains why nothing breaks: the new queries use their own cache keys, and neither one runs until a valid ticker is entered.
    • Files changed: a table listing each file with a one-line note on what changed in it.

    The final table deserves a closer inspection.

    FILE TAG CHANGE src/store/dashboardStore.js Modified Added customSymbol: '' state and the setCustomSymbol() action. Existing fields unchanged src/hooks/useMarketData.js Modified Added useCustomSymbolData(symbol), two parallel React Query calls for quote and history. Existing hooks unchanged src/components/dashboard/DashboardPage.jsx Modified Two new imports, two new store selectors, and a Custom Company section appended after the existing view switch. No existing JSX removed src/services/mock/quotes.json Modified NVDA quote entry appended. The existing five entries are left in place

    TREAT THE DESCRIPTION AS A DRAFT

    Read Bob's description before you paste it into GitHub. It is generated from the code Bob wrote and the tests that passed, so treat it the way you would a colleague's PR body: check that every claim matches what you saw in the browser in the previous module, and edit anything that overstates the change.

    SLASH COMMAND EQUIVALENTS

    If your Bob build exposes slash commands, this phase maps onto them directly: /review performs the diff review and surfaces findings, and /create-pr generates the description and prepares the pull request in one step. The prompt above demonstrates the same capabilities conversationally.

    Keep the report open. It provides you the text you will paste into the pull request in Step 3.

  1. Scroll to the Push commands block at the end of Bob's review. It contains three commands: one to stage the files, one to commit them with the message already written out, and one to push the branch.

    In the run shown, Bob produced this sequence:

    git add -A
git commit -m "feat: add user-selected company chart (CompanySelector + CustomSymbolPanel)

- customSymbol state in dashboardStore + setCustomSymbol action
- useCustomSymbolData hook (quote + 30-day history, mock-aware)
- CompanySelector: ticker input with 1-5 letter local validation
- CustomSymbolPanel: quote card + line chart, loading/error states
- NVDA mock fixture in quotes.json + history.json
- ResizeObserver polyfill in test setup
- 30 new tests: dashboardStore(12) CompanySelector(12) CustomSymbolPanel(6)
- 128/128 tests, 0 ESLint warnings, Vite build clean

Closes #1"

git push -u origin feature/user-selected-company-chart

    Two things to note before you run it:

    • The whole commit message sits inside one pair of quotes, so the block can be pasted and run as it is.
    • The last line, Closes #1, is what makes GitHub close the issue when this work is merged.

    Copy the block, paste it into a Terminal console, and hit Enter to execute.

    Check the output:

    • Your commit was protected by Block Secrets powered by IBM Vault Radar: the workspace scanned your files for passwords and keys before allowing the commit. This runs on every commit and is not a problem with your code.
    • [feature/user-selected-company-chart f36b1c4] feat: add user-selected company chart ...: the branch name and the new commit ID. The work went onto the feature branch, not main.
    • 62 files changed: how big the commit is.
    • The file list, where create mode 100644 marks a new file. Look for CompanySelector.jsx, CompanySelector.module.css, CustomSymbolPanel.jsx, and CustomSymbolPanel.module.css. Those four are the new feature.

    CHECK WHAT YOU ARE COMMITTING FIRST

    git add -A stages every changed file without asking. Run git status before you commit and read the list. If it includes anything you did not mean to deliver, add files one at a time with git add <path> instead.

    The push runs straight after the commit and sends the branch to GitHub, which starts CI.

  1. Open the pull request on GitHub. Refresh the repository page in your browser. GitHub shows a banner at the top of the file list saying the branch had recent pushes, with a green Compare & pull request button — click it.

    Note that main still shows the commit from the previous module. Your new work is on the feature branch, and the pull request is the request to bring it into main.

    IF THE BANNER IS NOT THERE

    The banner disappears after a while. Open the Pull requests tab, click New pull request, then set the base to main and the compare branch to feature/user-selected-company-chart. That opens the same form.

    The Open a pull request form already has two things in it. GitHub fills the title and description from your commit. Below that is the repository's own template from .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md, with empty Summary, Linked Issue, Changes, Test Coverage, Validation, Screenshots / Data Snapshots, and Notes for Reviewer headings.

    Fill in each heading using Bob's report from Step 1:

    TEMPLATE SECTION WHAT TO PASTE FROM BOB'S REPORT Summary The feature summary: what the new section does and what it renders Linked Issue Closes #1, so the merge closes the issue Changes The files-changed table, one bullet per file Test Coverage The new tests, and tick the three checkboxes Validation The check results: lint clean, all tests passing, clean build

    FINISH THE Closes # LINE

    The template includes an empty Closes # under Linked Issue. Change it to Closes #1 or delete the line. On its own, Closes # does not link to anything.

    When the description is ready, click Create pull request.

    The pull request is now open. Its header tells you:

    • The pull request number and the green Open badge.
    • Who wants to merge what, and in which direction: one commit, from feature/user-selected-company-chart into main.
    • The tabs: Commits, Checks, and Files changed, with the number of added and removed lines. The file count matches what the terminal reported in Step 2.
    • Able to merge at the top right, and Closes #1 as a working link to the issue.

    CHECK THAT THE ISSUE IS LINKED

    Look at the Development panel in the right sidebar. If the link worked, GitHub lists issue #1 there under Successfully merging this pull request may close these issues.

    If it says None yet, edit the description so there is exactly one Closes #1 on its own line, then save. This link is what closes the issue when you merge in Step 6.

  1. Let GitHub run the checks. Scroll to the bottom of the Conversation tab. Below the description is a panel reporting Some checks haven't completed yet.

    There are two entries, and both come from the workflow file you pushed in module 2-1:

    • Finance App CI / validate (push) — already finished. This ran when you pushed the commit in Step 2, because the branch name matches the feature/** pattern in the workflow's push trigger.
    • Finance App CI / validate (pull_request) — still running. This one started when you opened the pull request against main, which matches the workflow's second trigger.

    Below them, GitHub says No conflicts with base branch, which means it can merge the branch automatically once the checks finish.

    Click the Finance App CI check name (or Details beside it) to open the run.

    This is the validate job running, one step per line. Click any step to see its log. The first steps set up the machine: it checks out your branch, installs Node, then runs npm ci to install the dependencies from package-lock.json. The three checks are queued below and greyed out until their turn: Run npm run lint, Run npm run test:ci, and Run npm run build.

    The log says Node 20 is being deprecated. That is GitHub retiring the version its own actions run on. It has nothing to do with your application.

    It also says npm cache is not found. That is expected on a first run: there is nothing cached yet, so npm ci downloads everything. Later runs are faster.

    Wait for the job to finish, then reload.

    The validate job succeeded, with a green check on every step. Click Run npm run lint and the log shows the command GitHub ran:

    > finance-app@0.1.0 lint
> eslint src --ext .js,.jsx --report-unused-disable-directives --max-warnings 0

    Bob validated the code locally, but the merge decision rests on CI results no agent can edit and a review no agent can skip.

    That is the same command Bob ran in the previous module, now run on a fresh machine that has never seen your workspace. With Run npm run test:ci and Run npm run build green as well, all three checks Bob ran locally have passed again on GitHub.

  1. Back in the Bob IDE, ask Bob to confirm the branch is finished. Copy and paste the following prompt:

    Summarize the completed enhancement, confirm the branch is ready, and describe the final GitHub action needed to merge or close the request.

    Press Send. Bob runs git show --stat HEAD first so the summary is based on the commit that actually exists, then reports back that everything is confirmed. It produces a report titled SDLC Loop Closure — User-Selected Company Chart. Click Open.

    This report is the summary of everything the workshop produced.

    The header gives the commit and the branch, tagged Ready to merge and Closes #1. Below it, four tiles show the totals: tests passing, new tests added, ESLint warnings, and acceptance criteria met.

    The Enhancement summary describes the feature in plain terms: a user enters a ticker and gets a quote card and a 30-day price chart, in a Custom Company section below the existing dashboards. It then covers the rest of the behaviour, including validation before any network call, the loading and error states, the Clear button, the symbol surviving tab switches, and the NVDA fixture for offline use.

    Two columns list the new files and the changed ones:

    NEW FILES MODIFIED CompanySelector.jsx + .module.css dashboardStore.js, customSymbol state and action CustomSymbolPanel.jsx + .module.css useMarketData.js, the useCustomSymbolData hook dashboardStore.test.js (12 tests) DashboardPage.jsx, custom section wired below the views CompanySelector.test.jsx (12 tests) mock/quotes.json and mock/history.json, NVDA appended CustomSymbolPanel.test.jsx (6 tests) tests/setup.js, the ResizeObserver polyfill

    That is a much shorter list than the file count in the commit, because git counts every file the session rewrote while this report lists only the files the feature actually needed. If someone asks what this change consists of, the table above is the answer.

    The report ends with Full SDLC journey — steps completed, which walks back through the lab stage by stage: the issue Bob fetched, the acceptance criteria it defined, the implementation, the validation, and the delivery.

    Bob also posts the same summary in the sidebar, so you can read it without opening the report.

    It starts with Enhancement complete, branch is merge-ready, recaps what was built, and lists four reasons the change is safe: CompanySelector validates the ticker before any network call; CustomSymbolPanel only appears once a symbol is entered and reuses the existing SummaryCard and LineChart unchanged; useCustomSymbolData uses its own cache keys, so it cannot affect the existing queries; and customSymbol is stored in Zustand, so it survives tab switches.

    Below that, the Branch state table lists what Bob checked against git:

    CHECK RESULT Commit The commit ID and message Working tree 0 untracked or modified files ESLint 0 errors, 0 warnings Tests All passing, with no regressions Build Completed successfully Acceptance criteria All met, with passing tests

    The row to check before merging is Working tree: 0 untracked or modified files. It means there are no changes left on your machine that GitHub has not seen, so the CI run in Step 4 tested exactly the code you are about to merge.

  1. Merge the pull request. Open the repository on GitHub and click the Pull requests tab in the header.

    The list shows open pull requests only. The single entry is the one you created, with a green check because its checks passed and a 3 tasks counter from the checkboxes you ticked in the template. Click the title to open it.

    Review the change one final time before merging. Open the Files changed tab and compare it against Bob's report from Step 5. You should find the two new components, the store field, the hook, the fixtures, and the tests, and nothing else.

    Then go back to the Conversation tab and scroll to the merge box at the bottom.

    Both entries are green now: All checks have passed, with 2 successful checks where Step 4 had one still running, and No conflicts with base branch. Click Merge pull request.

    GitHub asks you to confirm and shows the merge commit it will create.

    GitHub fills in the Commit message and Extended description for you. Leave both as they are and click Confirm merge.

    The badge at the top turns purple and reads Merged, and the header now says the commit was merged into main. The feature is now part of the main branch.

    Next, check what the merge did to the issue. Click the Issues tab.

    The default view shows open issues, and it now reports Open 0 with No results. Click the Closed filter to see where the issue went.

    Issue #1, Add a graph for a user selected company, is marked closed, with a link on the right to the pull request that closed it. You never closed it yourself. The Closes #1 in the description did that when you merged.

    IF YOUR ISSUE IS STILL OPEN

    The Closes #1 line did not register. Close the issue by hand, and next time add it to the description before you create the pull request.

    The loop is complete: a GitHub issue went in, and a merged feature came out, checked by CI and linked back to the issue. The next enhancement follows the same path: new issue, new branch, new analysis, new pull request.

docs.title: iii. Complete SDLC coverage with Bob + GitHub
docs.text:
Across the two parts of this workshop, every stage of the software development lifecycle appeared, and Bob took part in each one:

SDLC STAGE WHERE IT HAPPENED OUTCOME 1. Planning & Requirements Bob fetched and analyzed the GitHub issue (previous module) Requirements understanding and acceptance criteria 2. Design & Architecture Bob identified the UI, state, and data service change areas Implementation plan that preserves existing features 3. Implementation Bob implemented the new company chart Working code that satisfies the requirements 4. Testing & QA Bob ran lint, tests, and build locally Verified functionality with passing gates 5. Code Review Bob reviewed the diff before delivery (/review) Findings surfaced before a human reviewer's time is spent 6. Integration Preparation Bob generated the commit message and PR description Clean commits and a description ready for review 7. Release Management The pull request opened against main (/create-pr) PR ready for maintainer review and merge 8. Continuous Integration GitHub Actions validated the push and the PR Automated lint, test, and build verification 9. Maintenance & Evolution The loop repeats for every new issue Continuous product evolution with Bob's assistance

Every change also traces back to the request that started it:

GitHub Issue Created
       ↓
Bob Fetches & Analyzes the Request
       ↓
Bob Implements the Feature
       ↓
Bob Runs Tests & Validation
       ↓
Bob Reviews the Changes
       ↓
Bob Prepares the Pull Request
       ↓
GitHub Actions CI/CD Validates
       ↓
Human Maintainer Reviews & Merges
       ↓
Feature Deployed and Issue Closed Automatically

docs.title: iv. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Finishing the work can be automated too. Reviewing the changes, writing the pull request description, and preparing the push are all things Bob can do.
  • Closes #N in the pull request description is the cheapest traceability available. Merging the work closes the request that asked for it.
  • Running the checks again on GitHub is what makes the work trustworthy. Passing locally is a claim whereas passing on CI is proof.
  • The merge is left to a person by design: Bob prepares the delivery, GitHub validates it, and a human-in-the-loop makes the decision.
  • The loop repeats. Every future enhancement follows the same path: issue, analysis, implementation, validation, pull request, merge.

Congratulations on completing this hands-on curriculum! In Part 1 | Build you planned and built an application with Bob; in Part 2 | Evolve you published it to GitHub and carried a real feature request from an open issue to a merged pull request.

Step back and consider what that loop demonstrates: the discipline of the AI Maturity Curve, operating inside the delivery platform your clients already use. Bob performing the work at every stage, and the human deciding what ships. That pairing is the story worth carrying into your next conversation about AI-assisted delivery.
